title: A New Kind of Value
content:
What problem does this solve?
A class describes a kind of object your program can create. An instance is one actual object made from that class. For this first lesson, think of a class as defining a new category of value and each instance as its own record.

Create two separate objects
  class Note:
      pass
  first = Note()
  second = Note()
Note is the class. first and second are separate instances.

Per-instance attributes
  first.text = "hello"
  second.text = "goodbye"
Each object can store different attribute values.

One-lesson microscope
This lesson assigns attributes after object creation only to isolate class-versus-instance thinking. It is not the final setup pattern. Lesson 26 immediately replaces this repetition with `__init__`.

Vocabulary after the behavior
A class describes a type of object. An instance (or object) is one value created from the class. An attribute is data stored on an object and accessed with dot syntax.
concepts: A class describes a kind of object
An instance is one separate object created from a class
Different instances can store different attribute values
Attributes are read/written through the instance with dot syntax
Classes are modeling tools, not mandatory replacements for simple dictionaries

examples.title: Create two instances
examples.code:
class Note:
    pass

first = Note()
second = Note()
examples.explanation: One class can create many separate instances.

examples.title: Different instance data
examples.code:
class Note:
    pass
first = Note()
second = Note()
first.text = "hello"
second.text = "goodbye"
print(first.text)
print(second.text)
examples.explanation: Each object stores its own text attribute.

common_mistakes: Calling the class itself one individual character
Assuming instances share attribute values simply because they share a class
Putting per-object state on the class itself
Assuming classes are automatically better than dictionaries
Trying to introduce inheritance before basic object state is understood

exercises.title: Class or instance?
exercises.prompt: In `class Note: ...` followed by `first = Note()`, which statement is correct?
choices: Note is the class; first is an instance.
first is the class; Note is an instance.
Both names refer to the same object.
hints: Look at which name appears after the `class` keyword.
Calling that class with parentheses creates an instance.
Note is the class; first is an instance.

exercises.title: Create two objects
exercises.prompt: Define an empty `Marker` class and create two instances named `first` and `second`. Do not use `__init__` yet.
exercises.reference_solution:
class Marker:
    pass

first = Marker()
second = Marker()
hints: The class definition is already enough to make instances in this lesson.
Call Marker() twice and store each result under a different name.
Use `first = Marker()` and `second = Marker()`.

exercises.title: Give each object a value
exercises.prompt: Set `first.value = 1` and `second.value = 2`, then print both values on separate lines.
exercises.starter_code:
class Marker:
    pass
first = Marker()
second = Marker()

# Assign different value attributes.
exercises.reference_solution:
class Marker:
    pass
first = Marker()
second = Marker()
first.value = 1
second.value = 2
print(first.value)
print(second.value)
hints: Attributes belong to a specific instance, so use the object name before the dot.
Assign one value through first and the other through second.
Use `first.value = 1` and `second.value = 2`, then print them.

exercises.title: Independent attributes
exercises.code_to_predict:
class Box:
    pass
a = Box()
b = Box()
a.label = "A"
b.label = "B"
a.label = "Changed"
print(b.label)
hints: a and b are separate instances.
The later assignment changes only a.label.
b.label remains B.

exercises.title: Dictionary or object?
exercises.prompt: You have one simple dictionary record used only for key lookup. Must it be converted to a class immediately?
choices: Yes; classes always replace dictionaries once learned.
No; a dictionary can remain clearer when object behavior/responsibility is not needed.
hints: New syntax is not automatically a better model.
Ask whether the record benefits from object identity or related behavior.
A plain dictionary can still be the clearer choice.

exercises.title: Change the intended instance
exercises.prompt: The goal is for only `second.health` to become 7. Repair the final assignment and keep first.health at 10.
exercises.starter_code:
class Unit:
    pass
first = Unit()
second = Unit()
first.health = 10
second.health = 10
first.health = 7
exercises.reference_solution:
class Unit:
    pass
first = Unit()
second = Unit()
first.health = 10
second.health = 10
second.health = 7
hints: The class is not the problem; trace which instance the final line targets.
The requirement says only second should change.
Change the final assignment to `second.health = 7`.

exercises.title: Neutral record objects
exercises.prompt: Define an empty `Player` class. In `build_players()`, create two Player instances with different `name` and `score` attributes and return them in a list. Use names `Ada`/`Bo` and scores 3/7. Do not use `__init__` yet.
exercises.reference_solution:
class Player:
    pass

def build_players():
    first = Player()
    first.name = "Ada"
    first.score = 3
    second = Player()
    second.name = "Bo"
    second.score = 7
    return [first, second]
hints: Create each Player separately inside the function before assigning its attributes.
Give the two instances different name/score values, then put the objects themselves in a list.
Return `[first, second]` after assigning Ada/3 and Bo/7.

exercises.title: First Character Objects
exercises.prompt: Define an empty `Character` class. `make_party()` must create separate Aria and Rook instances with `name`, `health`, and `inventory`: Aria/10/[] and Rook/14/[]. Then mutate Aria before returning: set aria.health to 8 and append `"rope"` to aria.inventory. Return `[aria, rook]`. Rook must remain health 14 with an empty, separate inventory. Do not use `__init__` yet.
exercises.reference_solution:
class Character:
    pass

def make_party():
    aria = Character()
    aria.name = "Aria"
    aria.health = 10
    aria.inventory = []

    rook = Character()
    rook.name = "Rook"
    rook.health = 14
    rook.inventory = []

    aria.health = 8
    aria.inventory.append("rope")
    return [aria, rook]
hints: Create two Character() calls, not one object stored under two names.
Give each instance its own literal `[]` inventory before mutating Aria.
After Aria receives rope and health 8, return both objects. Hidden checks will verify Rook stayed unchanged and the inventories are different objects.

tests.expression: (lambda p: [p[0].name, p[0].health, p[0].inventory, p[1].name, p[1].health, p[1].inventory])(make_party())

exercises.success_message: Aria and Rook are separate Character instances with independent mutable inventory state.
